faq.a: Start frequent, low‑stimulus care and obtain a baseline Finnegan score; treat pharmacologically only if the score reaches ≥ 8.
faq.q: What is the most important initial step when NAS is suspected?

faq.a: Continuing maternal methadone can stabilise the infant’s exposure and reduce the severity of withdrawal.
faq.q: Why is methadone sometimes continued in the mother after delivery?

faq.a: Yes, if the mother is on a stable opioid maintenance dose and not using illicit drugs; breastfeeding can lessen withdrawal severity.
faq.q: Can a newborn with NAS be breast‑fed?

exam: A newborn of a mother on methadone shows tremor, high‑pitched cry and poor feeding on day 2 – what is your next step? — Obtain a Finnegan score, start non‑pharmacologic care, and if score ≥ 8 begin opioid weaning.
How does the Finnegan scoring system guide treatment decisions? — Scores ≥ 8 indicate pharmacologic therapy; serial scores track response and weaning.
Why is phenobarbital not the first drug of choice for NAS? — It can mask seizures, prolong withdrawal, and has a long half‑life leading to sedation.

A baby with suspected NAS has a normal glucose but is lethargic – what alternative diagnoses should you consider? — Sepsis, hypoxic‑ischemic injury, metabolic disorder; obtain cultures and basic labs.
In a low‑resource hospital without toxicology, how do you confirm NAS? — Rely on detailed maternal drug history and serial Finnegan scoring; treat based on clinical severity.
What non‑pharmacologic measures reduce the need for medication in NAS? — Swaddling, low‑light environment, frequent small feeds, skin‑to‑skin contact, and minimizing handling.
Explain the rationale for using oral morphine rather than long‑acting opioids in NAS. — Short‑acting agents allow rapid titration and easier weaning, reducing prolonged exposure.
A neonate on clonidine for refractory NAS becomes hypotensive – what is your immediate action? — Stop clonidine, provide fluid bolus and consider vasopressor support if needed.
ai.title: Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS) is a withdrawal syndrome in newborns after in‑utero exposure to opioids or other substances. It presents with autonomic, gastrointestinal and neurologic signs that vary in severity.

b: Incidence highest where opioid use in pregnancy is common; rising in many low‑resource settings.
Most common cause: maternal use of heroin, methadone or buprenorphine.
sections.p: NAS occurs when a fetus is chronically exposed to opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, nicotine or certain antiretrovirals and then loses that exposure at birth. The syndrome reflects the infant’s adaptation to the sudden absence of the drug.

b: Peak severity usually by day 3‑5 for opioids, earlier for nicotine.
sections.p: The clinical picture follows a predictable timeline: early signs (within 24 h) are usually autonomic, later signs (48‑72 h) involve the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Severity is graded by the Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System.

b: Risk of rapid weight loss > 10 % of birth weight.
Potential for respiratory distress if untreated.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents complications such as feeding failure, dehydration, seizures and prolonged hospital stay. In low‑resource hospitals, careful bedside assessment often replaces laboratory confirmation.

t.b: Identifies likely offending substance; guides monitoring frequency.
Confirms exposure; if unavailable, rely on clinical scoring.
Detects hypoglycaemia, a common early complication; treat if < 2.5 mmol/L.
Assesses dehydration and renal impairment; treat accordingly.

b: Non‑pharmacologic: swaddling, low‑stimulus environment, frequent small feeds, skin‑to‑skin contact.
First‑line drug: oral morphine or diluted tincture of opium; chosen for predictable titration and short half‑life.
Avoid phenobarbital as initial agent because it can mask seizures and prolong withdrawal.
If opioid therapy fails, consider clonidine (alpha‑2 agonist) – used only where monitoring for hypotension is possible.
sections.p: Treat the cause first (e.g., continue maternal opioid if on methadone maintenance) then provide supportive care. Pharmacologic therapy is reserved for moderate‑severe cases.

b: Sepsis: fever, lethargy, poor feeding but usually with elevated CRP and positive cultures.
Hypoglycaemia: similar jitteriness; confirmed by low glucose.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic NAS include sepsis, hypoxic‑ischemic encephalopathy, metabolic disorders and congenital infections.

b: Maternal nicotine exposure may cause tremor and irritability but scores are often < 8; still monitor closely.
sections.p: A low Finnegan score early in the course does not rule out later worsening; repeat scoring every 4‑6 h.

b: Explain why non‑pharmacologic measures are first‑line.
State the Finnegan threshold for starting medication.
Discuss safe weaning of opioid therapy.
sections.p: Examiners test ability to recognise, grade and manage NAS, especially in resource‑limited settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid weight loss > 15 % of birth weight
